title: The Capillary Trap: How Blood Cells Squeeze to Live

shots.narration: Human capillaries are mere hair-thin tunnels, half the diameter of the blood cells entering them.
shots.start_visual: Nucleus Medical Media 9:16 vertical shot: endoscopic view inside a narrowing arteriole branching into microscopic capillaries, strictly zero text.
shots.end_visual: Approaching the tiny six-micrometer capillary entrance where blood plasma accelerates into the bottleneck, strictly zero text.

shots.narration: An eight-micrometer red blood cell must physically deform to squeeze into the narrow passage.
shots.start_visual: Vertical view of an eight-micrometer biconcave disc red blood cell approaching the six-micrometer vessel mouth, strictly zero text.
shots.end_visual: Pushing closer as the flexible red cell compresses against the entrance, folding like a parachute, strictly zero text.

shots.narration: Inside the cell membrane, elastic spectrin protein networks stretch without breaking under crushing pressures.
shots.start_visual: Macro cutaway through erythrocyte membrane: glowing hexagonal spectrin protein cytoskeleton stretching under tension, strictly zero text.
shots.end_visual: Zooming into the flexible protein coils as they deform smoothly without tearing or losing structural integrity, strictly zero text.

shots.narration: Tightly pressed against the vessel wall, the cell unloads oxygen molecules in milliseconds.
shots.start_visual: Close-up inside the capillary: folded red blood cell sliding against glistening endothelial wall, strictly zero text.
shots.end_visual: Focus pulling to glowing cyan oxygen molecules diffusing across the ultra-thin vessel wall into tissue, strictly zero text.

shots.narration: Exiting the bottleneck into wider venules, the resilient cell snaps back into shape.
